h4: Pick the craft you keep thinking about. Curiosity is the best teacher we have.
p: Clay, ink, yarn or silver? A short guide to picking the craft that fits how you like to spend an afternoon.
We get this question every week: which class should I start with? There is no wrong answer, but there is usually a best one for you.
Start with ceramics. Wheel Throwing I is messy, physical and very satisfying. You will be covered in clay within ten minutes, and you will leave with two pieces to glaze.
Hands at work in the studio
Try linocut. If you already sketch or doodle, printmaking turns your drawings into something you can print again and again.
Weaving and natural dyeing are slower and quieter. They suit people who want an afternoon to switch off, with something soft and colourful at the end.
Silver Ring Making takes a single afternoon, and you walk out wearing a finished ring sized to fit.
The bench, set for a class
Still unsure? Write to us and a tutor will reply the same day.

/journal/a-year-in-the-dye-garden.title: A year in the dye garden — Handsel Journal
/journal/a-year-in-the-dye-garden.description: Weld, madder and woad grow in the yard behind the textile room. This is how a handful of plants gives us a whole season of colour.
h1: A year in the dye garden
h2: Autumn and winter: the dye pots
h3: Five things to know before your first linocut
How to make a ring that actually fits
What happens to your pot after you leave
Open evenings are back for autumn
h4: The same plant gives a different colour every year. I’ve stopped trying to repeat it and started enjoying it.
p: Weld, madder and woad grow in the yard behind the textile room. This is how a handful of plants gives us a whole season of colour.
Behind the textile room there is a strip of ground no bigger than two parking spaces. Four years ago it was gravel. Now it grows most of the colour we use in our natural dyeing classes.

We sow woad for blues, weld for bright yellows and dyer’s chamomile for softer golds. Madder, which gives us reds and pinks, takes three years before its roots are ready, so it gets its own bed and a lot of patience.
Lifting cloth out of the indigo vat
Weld is cut just as it flowers. We hang it in bundles in the drying room, and for a few weeks the whole studio smells faintly of hay.
Weld: yellows, and greens over blue
Madder root: corals, reds and pinks
Most of our dyeing happens in the colder months, once the harvest is dry and stored. Wool and silk take colour most readily; linen and cotton need a little more preparation first.
In class you dye a set of skeins from the garden and take home a small sample book with notes on every pot.
Grows half of the dye garden herself.

/journal/five-things-to-know-before-your.title: Five things to know before your first linocut — Handsel Journal
/journal/five-things-to-know-before-your.description: Carving in reverse, sharp tools and the joy of the first pull. A few notes to help your first print go smoothly.
h1: Five things to know before your first linocut
h2: 2. You carve away what you don’t want
5. The first print is a test
h3: A year in the dye garden
Open evenings are back for autumn
How to make a ring that actually fits
What happens to your pot after you leave
h4: Pull the first print, look at it, then carve again. The block tells you what it needs.
p: Carving in reverse, sharp tools and the joy of the first pull. A few notes to help your first print go smoothly.
Linocut is one of the most forgiving ways into printmaking. You need a block, a few gouges and some ink. Still, a few things surprise almost everyone in their first session.
Whatever you carve appears mirrored on the paper. That matters most for letters and numbers. We trace your design, flip it and transfer it, so the print comes out the right way round.
The surface you leave untouched holds the ink, and everything you cut stays white. It takes a moment to think this way, so we start with bold shapes and keep fine lines for later.
Gouges are sharp. Always carve away from the hand holding the block, and use the bench hook we give you. Short, shallow cuts give you more control than one deep one.
A thin, even layer that looks like velvet on the roller prints best. Too much ink fills your fine lines and blurs the edges.
Pulling a print in the print room
Most people make three or four proofs before they are happy. That isn’t failure. That is printmaking.

/journal/forty-years-at-the-bench.description: Peter Lund made his first ring in 1986 and has taught at Handsel since the start. We asked him what has changed, and what never does.
h3: How to choose your first class
A year in the dye garden
How to make a ring that actually fits
What happens to your pot after you leave
Open evenings are back for autumn
h4: Silver is patient. It will let you fix almost anything if you slow down.
p: Peter Lund made his first ring in 1986 and has taught at Handsel since the start. We asked him what has changed, and what never does.
Peter’s bench is the one by the window, with hammer handles worn smooth and a jar of offcuts he refuses to throw away. He has been making jewellery for forty years and teaching for nearly twenty.
“By accident. I was repairing watches and someone asked if I could resize a ring. I made a mess of it, went to an evening class to learn how to do it properly, and never really stopped.”
Setting a stone at the jewellery bench
“They rush the filing. Soldering is the exciting part, so everyone wants to get there, but a good join starts with two ends that meet perfectly. Ten more minutes with a file saves an hour later.”

“The tools are better and the lamps are brighter. People are different too. Twenty years ago my students wanted a hobby. Now a lot of them want a break from screens, something they can hold at the end of the day.”
“The moment someone puts on a ring they made themselves. Every single time, they go quiet for a second. I still look forward to that.”
Forty years at the bench and still learning.

/journal/what-happens-to-your-pot-after-.title: What happens to your pot after you leave — Handsel Journal
/journal/what-happens-to-your-pot-after-.description: Your pot isn't finished when the class ends. Here is the three-week journey from wet clay to a glazed piece you can eat from.
h1: What happens to your pot after you leave
h2: Days one to five: leather hard
h3: Open evenings are back for autumn
How to make a ring that actually fits
Five things to know before your first linocut
h4: Nobody opens a kiln without holding their breath a little. After twelve years, I still do.
p: Your pot isn't finished when the class ends. Here is the three-week journey from wet clay to a glazed piece you can eat from.

Most people leave their first wheel class with clay under their nails and a slightly wonky cylinder on a board. Three weeks later, that cylinder comes back as something you can drink from. Here is what happens in between.

Fresh pots are full of water, so they rest on a shelf under loose plastic. Slow drying matters: if one side dries faster than the other, the pot can warp or crack. After a few days the clay reaches leather hard, firm enough to hold its shape but still soft enough to carve.

This is when we trim. Your pot goes back on the wheel upside down, and a tutor shaves away the extra clay at the base to give it a neat foot ring. If you come back for a trimming session, you can do this part yourself.
Throwing a cylinder in the wheel room

Once it is completely dry, your pot goes into the kiln for a bisque firing at around 1000°C. It takes most of a day to heat up and another to cool down. The clay turns pale, hard and slightly porous, ready to soak up glaze.

You choose a glaze from our test wall, and we dip, pour or brush it on. The second firing goes hotter, up to 1260°C, where the glaze melts into glass and the clay becomes stoneware: dense, strong and safe for food.
Bisque firing: about 1000°C, a day to cool
Glaze firing: up to 1260°C, another full day
Collection: usually three weeks after your class
Mugs taking shape on the wheel
We send a message when your pieces are ready. Bring a bag, and maybe a friend who will pretend to be impressed.
Throws every morning before the first class arrives.

/journal/how-to-make-a-ring-that-actuall.title: How to make a ring that actually fits — Handsel Journal
/journal/how-to-make-a-ring-that-actuall.description: Fingers swell in summer, shrink in the cold and are rarely the same size on both hands. Peter’s guide to sizing a ring you will want to wear every day.
h1: How to make a ring that actually fits
h3: What happens to your pot after you leave
Open evenings are back for autumn
Five things to know before your first linocut
h4: A ring should go over the knuckle with a little push and then sit still. If it spins, it is too big.
p: Fingers swell in summer, shrink in the cold and are rarely the same size on both hands. Peter’s guide to sizing a ring you will want to wear every day.
Most rings that end up in a drawer were never really the wrong design. They were the wrong size. Here is how we make sure the ring you make at the bench is one you will wear every day.

Fingers change through the day. They swell when it is warm and after exercise, and shrink in the cold. We size at the start of class, once your hands have warmed up, and check again just before we cut the silver.
Trying on ring sizers at the bench
A wide band fits tighter than a thin one of the same size, because it covers more of the finger. For anything wider than six millimetres, we usually go up half a size.
Thin bands up to 3 mm: your usual size
Medium bands, 4 to 6 mm: your usual size or a quarter up
Wide bands over 6 mm: half a size up
If a finished ring is a touch tight, we can stretch it on a steel mandrel by up to half a size. Going smaller means cutting and soldering again, so it is always better to start slightly snug.
Stretching a band on the mandrel
Not sure of your size before you book? Ask for a sizer when you arrive, or measure an old ring that fits and bring the number with you.

/about.title: About Handsel — Our Story in Bristol
/about.description: Four rooms, a team of working makers and a kettle that is usually on. How a single pottery wheel became Handsel.
p: Four rooms, working makers, and a kettle that is usually on.
Handsel began with one wheel in a railway arch. Today it is four rooms where people learn to make things properly, by hand.
From a borrowed railway arch to four rooms, a dye garden and a kiln that rarely gets a night off.
Handsel began in 2014 with one pottery wheel in a shared railway arch. The printmakers came next, then a weaver who planted a dye garden, and finally a jeweller who needed a bench by the window.
Friends asked to try the wheel, then their friends did. Within a year the waiting list was longer than the room.
Small groups, real tools and enough time to make something you are proud of.
A borrowed railway arch, one second-hand wheel and a kettle.
A Columbian press arrives on a pallet and needs six people to lift.
Ada plants madder, weld and woad. The indigo vat is still alive.
Peter joins with six benches and a very calm voice.
Twelve classes a week, an open studio and a kiln that rarely rests.
Each craft has its own room, its own tools and its own tutor. Most students end up trying a second one.
Wheel, hand-building and glazing in a studio with six wheels and two kilns.
Linocut, screen printing and risograph on presses you can book after your first class.
Weaving, natural dyeing and embroidery, with plant-dyed yarn from our own dye garden.
Ring making, stone setting and casting at fully equipped benches.
Never more than eight people at a bench, so your tutor actually sees your hands and not just your back.
Every tutor runs their own practice. You learn the real way of doing things, shortcuts included.
Classes are long enough to make something whole. We fire, glaze and keep your work until it is ready.
Four tutors, one for each craft. Ask them anything; they love talking shop.
